concepts.name: Constitutional Basis and Genesis of PESA Act
key_dimensions: Article 243M: exclusion of Scheduled Areas from Part IX (Panchayats) and the need for special legislation
Fifth Schedule vs Sixth Schedule distinction — PESA applies only to Fifth Schedule areas, NOT Sixth Schedule areas
Bhuria Committee (1994–95) recommendations that led to PESA enactment in 1996
PESA as an enabling/framework legislation requiring state governments to enact conforming laws

concepts.name: Geographical Scope and Applicability of PESA
key_dimensions: Applies to 10 states with Fifth Schedule areas: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan
Northeastern tribal states (Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, etc.) are excluded as they fall under Sixth Schedule
PESA does NOT apply to union territories or non-scheduled tribal areas
Distinction between 'Scheduled Area' (Presidential notification under Fifth Schedule) and 'Tribal Area' under Sixth Schedule

concepts.name: Gram Sabha as the Foundation Unit under PESA
key_dimensions: PESA places Gram Sabha (not Gram Panchayat) at the centre — it is competent to safeguard and preserve traditions, customs, cultural identity
Gram Sabha's mandatory approval for land acquisition, resettlement, and rehabilitation in Scheduled Areas
Gram Sabha's power to manage minor forest produce, water bodies, and minor minerals
Distinction: Under regular Part IX, Gram Panchayat is the key body; under PESA, Gram Sabha is supreme — a common UPSC trap

concepts.name: Powers of Gram Sabha over Natural Resources
key_dimensions: Ownership rights of Gram Sabha over minor forest produce (MFP) — confirmed and expanded by Forest Rights Act 2006
Mandatory consultation with Gram Sabha before grant of prospecting licences or mining leases for minor minerals
Control over money-lending to tribals and management of local markets
Interplay with Forest Rights Act 2006: PESA + FRA together create a robust framework but overlap creates confusion in implementation

concepts.name: PESA and Land Alienation: Protection of Tribal Land Rights
key_dimensions: State legislatures must prevent alienation of tribal land and restore unlawfully alienated land — mandatory, not discretionary
Gram Sabha's mandatory consultation before land acquisition in Scheduled Areas
Conflict with Land Acquisition Act (LARR Act 2013): LARR requires consent of 70–80% of affected families in Scheduled Areas — stronger than general areas
Supreme Court in Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997): government land in Scheduled Areas cannot be leased to non-tribals/private companies

concepts.name: PESA and Prohibition of Intoxicants
key_dimensions: Gram Sabha has the power to enforce prohibition or to regulate/restrict sale and consumption of liquor
This is often in conflict with state excise policies — a major implementation challenge
States like Andhra Pradesh and Chhattisgarh have faced controversies over overriding Gram Sabha decisions on liquor
Comparison with Directive Principle under Article 47 (prohibition of intoxicating drinks)

concepts.name: Reservation Provisions under PESA
key_dimensions: Chairpersons of panchayats at ALL levels in Scheduled Areas shall be reserved for Scheduled Tribes — mandatory provision
Not less than half of total seats in every panchayat to be reserved for Scheduled Tribes
Reservation of seats at every panchayat level for STs, SCs, and women — but ST reservation is the PESA-specific requirement
UPSC trap: In regular Part IX, reservation of chairperson posts is left to states; under PESA it is mandatory for STs

concepts.name: State Conformity Laws and Obligation under PESA
key_dimensions: Section 4 of PESA mandates that state legislations on panchayats in Scheduled Areas shall be in consonance with customary law, social and religious practices
States are obligated to amend their Panchayati Raj Acts to conform with PESA — many states have been slow or partial
No state has fully implemented PESA-conforming legislation — a persistent criticism
Rajasthan, Himachal Pradesh, Gujarat compliance status vs laggards — relevant for GS-II governance angle

concepts.name: PESA and Higher-Level Panchayat Powers Over Gram Sabha
key_dimensions: PESA explicitly restricts higher-level panchayats from assuming powers/authority that would compromise the Gram Sabha's position
No higher-level panchayat can supersede or override Gram Sabha decisions — UPSC often tests this hierarchy inversion
Contrast with regular Part IX where higher panchayat tiers generally have supervisory authority
Practical challenge: District-level bodies (collectors, DMs) often override Gram Sabhas — violation of PESA's spirit

concepts.name: PESA and Control over Money-Lending and Credit
key_dimensions: Gram Sabha has power to regulate money-lending to tribals — aimed at addressing debt bondage and exploitation
States must enact laws to give Gram Sabhas this authority but most have not done so effectively
Conflict with moneylenders operating outside formal banking: PESA tries to address but enforcement is weak
Linkage with Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 — overlapping protections

concepts.name: Minor Forest Produce (MFP): Ownership and Management
key_dimensions: PESA grants Gram Sabha ownership of minor forest produce (tendu leaves, mahua, sal seeds, etc.) — a departure from state forest department control
Forest Rights Act 2006 reinforced and expanded this right, including community forest resource rights
State governments often retain control through forest departments or cooperative structures — a conflict with PESA mandate
Definition of MFP under PESA vs FRA 2006: FRA broadened the definition to include all non-timber forest produce

concepts.name: PESA and Mining/Industrialisation Conflicts
key_dimensions: Mandatory prior consultation with Gram Sabha before prospecting/mining licences for minor minerals in Scheduled Areas
Supreme Court in Niyamgiri (Vedanta) Case (2013): upheld Gram Sabha's right to decide on mining — landmark application of PESA
PESA covers only 'minor minerals'; major minerals (coal, iron ore) fall under central law — a critical distinction and UPSC trap
Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act 2015 and its interface with PESA consent requirements

concepts.name: Relationship Between PESA and Fifth Schedule
key_dimensions: Fifth Schedule provides for Tribes Advisory Council (TAC) and Governor's special powers; PESA adds a grassroots democratic layer
Governor can direct that a central/state law shall not apply to a Scheduled Area — this power coexists but is separate from PESA
TAC advises on welfare of STs but has no direct relationship with PESA's Gram Sabha framework — potential confusion point
PESA does not replace Fifth Schedule protections; it supplements them from below (bottom-up vs top-down)

concepts.name: PESA vs Sixth Schedule: Key Structural Differences
key_dimensions: Sixth Schedule: autonomous district councils with legislative, executive, and judicial powers — more robust autonomy
PESA (Fifth Schedule areas): relies on state conformity laws and Gram Sabha empowerment — weaker enforcement
Sixth Schedule areas are explicitly excluded from PESA — applies to Northeast India tribal areas under separate framework
Demands to extend Sixth Schedule-type protections to Fifth Schedule areas — a recurring debate

concepts.name: Implementation Failures and Governance Challenges of PESA
key_dimensions: No state has enacted complete PESA-conforming legislation — key governance failure
Bureaucratic and political resistance: district administration often bypasses Gram Sabha for development projects
Awareness deficit among tribal communities about their rights under PESA — capacity-building gap
Xaxa Committee Report (2014) and Ministry of Tribal Affairs reviews highlighting systemic non-compliance

concepts.name: PESA and Peaceful Coexistence with Customary Law
key_dimensions: Section 4(a): state legislation must be in consonance with customary law, social and religious practices, and traditional management practices of community resources
Recognition of traditional governance institutions (like village councils under different tribal names) as valid Gram Sabhas
Tension between constitutional secular law and tribal customary practices (e.g., exclusion of women in some traditional councils)
PESA's balancing act: modernising governance while respecting indigenous traditions — a unique constitutional approach

concepts.name: PESA and Displacement/Rehabilitation Policy
key_dimensions: Mandatory consultation with Gram Sabha before land acquisition and resettlement of tribals from Scheduled Areas
LARR Act 2013 (Right to Fair Compensation Act): requires Social Impact Assessment (SIA) AND consent of Gram Sabha in Scheduled Areas — stronger protection than general areas
Nandini Sundar v. State of Chhattisgarh (2011): SC highlighted displacement and governance failures in Scheduled Areas
Conflict between 'development' imperatives (dams, highways, mines) and PESA's protective mandate — a classic GS-II dilemma

concepts.name: PESA and Police/Peace-Keeping Powers
key_dimensions: Gram Sabha has the authority to prevent alienation of land but also to maintain peace and public order at village level
Village-level peace committees and their relationship with formal police — PESA envisions a community policing role
Controversy: Salwa Judum (Chhattisgarh) and other state-sponsored armed groups seen as violating the spirit of PESA
SC in Nandini Sundar case (2011) struck down Salwa Judum partly on grounds of failure of constitutional governance in Scheduled Areas

concepts.name: PESA and Water Bodies/Fisheries Management
key_dimensions: Gram Sabha has management rights over minor water bodies for purposes like fishing, irrigation within Scheduled Areas
Conflict with state irrigation and fisheries departments that often auction water body rights ignoring Gram Sabha
FRA 2006 extends community rights to water bodies within community forest resource areas — overlap with PESA
Practical distinction: PESA covers management rights; ownership of water bodies still vests with the state — a nuanced point

concepts.name: Recent Developments and Amendments Related to PESA
key_dimensions: PESA Rules 2022 (notified by Centre for guidance) — first-ever model PESA rules to help states frame their own rules, 26 years after the Act
Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Himachal Pradesh among states that notified their PESA rules post-2022
2022 Rules strengthened Gram Sabha powers over MFP, money-lending, and land alienation — key provisions
Ongoing debate on bringing Scheduled Areas under direct Central monitoring and whether PESA needs a penal clause for non-compliance by states
